chunks.text: Editorial Header. The home screen opens with a large serif headline that rotates through a shuffled pool of dictate calls-to-action ("What do you want to dictate today?", "Talk faster than you type. Start here.", "Speak it straight into your last app.", and similar) in place of the former static "Recents." title, with today's date retained as a subtitle directly above the search bar and transcript list. The rotating line doubles as the home's quiet micro-messaging surface, gently coaching the speak-don't-type habit without an extra banner. The top row of the header carries only the circular brand logo (clipped from the app icon art) on the left — the "Jot" text wordmark was dropped, and the logo is sized to read at the same diameter as the Help and Settings glass buttons on the right so the three sit on one line. Cumulative dictation stats — typing time saved today, lifetime dictation count, and a 14-day sparkline — are surfaced in Settings → About rather than on the home page, keeping the home surface focused on recent activity.
chunks.title: Editorial Header

chunks.text: Transcript Library with Time Grouping. All past recordings are presented in a scrollable list automatically bucketed into four recency groups — Today, Yesterday, Last 7 days, and Earlier — so users can find recent notes without searching. Library entries include transcripts captured from any surface — the main app, the keyboard, Shortcuts, and the Apple Watch app — all interleaved by capture time. Each row shows the recording's timestamp, its duration when known (live dictations record it; file transcriptions via Shortcuts do not), and a two-line excerpt of the transcript text. The most recent entry is rendered as a featured one-line serif-italic quote on a soft blue-tinted card at the top of the list, so the newest transcript reads as the headline of the page; the recency label that introduces it (e.g. "Today") sits inside the same blue-tinted panel so the header and featured quote read as a single editorial section. Entries below the featured row, and all other recency sections, use the standard row treatment on the parent card surface. A small coral sparkles glyph appears alongside the timestamp on any row whose transcript has an AI Rewrite — a quiet, glanceable affordance that distinguishes rewritten entries from raw originals. The same coral sparkle appears on the keyboard Recents strip for visual parity. A few voice captures never land in the library by design — for example a Voice Prompt rewrite instruction is used once and never saved as a transcript.
chunks.title: Transcript Library with Time Grouping

chunks.text: Live Search. A persistent search bar at the top of the library filters the transcript list in real time as the user types, matching against both the displayed (cleaned/rewritten) text and the original raw transcript text, so any recording can be located by a remembered phrase regardless of which version it appears in.
chunks.title: Live Search

chunks.text: Home Empty State. When the library contains no transcripts, a dedicated empty state is shown in place of the list, inviting the user to make their first dictation.
chunks.title: Home Empty State

chunks.text: Home No-Search-Results State. When a search query is active but no transcripts match, a "No matches" message is shown with a suggestion to try a different search term.
chunks.title: Home No-Search-Results State

chunks.text:
Floating Dictate Button. A prominent blue floating action button labeled "Dictate" sits anchored at the bottom of the home screen. Tapping it navigates to the full-screen Recording Hero via a navigation push.

While a recording is in progress and the user has backed out of the recording surface, the Dictate button is replaced in place by a blue gradient "Recording" pill containing a pulsing white dot, the live elapsed timer, and a small upward arrow. Tapping the pill returns to the live recording surface; the pill carries a soft outer blue wash so it reads as live without dominating the home view.
chunks.title: Floating Dictate Button

chunks.text: Transcript Row Actions. Each transcript row supports a swipe-left gesture that reveals two actions — a red Delete for single-row removal and a Select action that enters multi-select mode with that row pre-selected — so multi-select is discoverable from the swipe rather than hidden. A long-press also enters multi-select (a secondary path) starting with the long-pressed row pre-selected. A short tap on a row opens the Transcript Detail view. Delete triggers a confirmation dialog before permanently removing the entry.
chunks.title: Transcript Row Actions

chunks.text: Help Access. A question-mark button in the home header opens the Help screen as a modal sheet, accessible at any time without leaving the library.
chunks.title: Help Access

chunks.text: Settings Access. A gear icon in the home header opens Settings as a modal sheet. It replaces the former profile-avatar circle — a gear reads plainly as "settings" without implying a user account, which Jot does not have.
chunks.title: Settings Access

chunks.text: Multi-Select & Combine. Multi-select mode is primarily discoverable from the swipe-left gesture on any transcript row, which reveals a Select action alongside Delete (see §1.7); tapping Select enters multi-select with that row pre-selected. A long-press on a row is kept as a secondary entry path (and the VoiceOver "Enter selection mode" action), also entering multi-select with the pressed row pre-selected. In this mode the Dictate button is replaced by a bottom toolbar with three actions: Select All (selects every visible transcript), Combine (merges 2 or more selected entries into one new transcript, no upper limit), and Delete N (removes all selected entries after a confirmation dialog). Tapping additional rows toggles their selection. Exit multi-select by completing an action or by tapping outside the selected rows. Combine is enabled once at least 2 rows are selected, with no upper limit on how many can be combined. Tapping Combine opens a confirmation dialog with two options: Combine and delete originals (destructive — the source entries are removed and replaced by the new combined one) and Combine and keep originals (the new combined entry is created alongside the originals). In both cases, the combined entry is built from the best available version of each source — if a source has an AI Rewrite, the rewrite is used; if it does not, the original transcript is used. The picked strings are joined oldest-first (the earliest dictation appears at the top of the combined entry, the most recent at the bottom) with paragraph breaks. This is the opposite of the library's visual order — the library shows newest on top — because the combined entry reads naturally as a chronological narrative rather than as a stack of the rows in display order. The result is stored as the new entry's original (the new combined entry has no Rewrite of its own and no Rewrite tab). The new entry receives a fresh timestamp and ledger number.
chunks.title: Multi-Select & Combine

chunks.text: Ask Jot Entry Point. A small sparkles pill sits next to the search bar in the home header. Where search finds a remembered phrase, this opens Ask Jot — natural-language Q&A across all the user's notes. The pill only appears once the device has a capable answer model available (see §14.6), so the entry point is never shown in a non-working state.
chunks.title: Ask Jot Entry Point

chunks.text: Light & Dark Appearance. The entire app follows the system Light / Dark setting automatically — the page wallpaper, Liquid-Glass cards, editorial type, and every text color shift to their dark variants over a near-black page, with no in-app appearance switch. The Jot Keyboard and Apple Watch app follow the same system appearance (the watch is always on a true-black backdrop). Brand, status, and semantic-icon colors stay constant across both modes; only surfaces, text inks, and keyboard chrome adapt.
chunks.title: Light & Dark Appearance

chunks.text:
Full-Screen Recording Surface. The app presents a dedicated full-screen recording view primarily in three cases: the user taps the home Dictate button; the user taps Dictate on the Jot Keyboard from another app with no Warm Hold active (a *cold* start — the surface opens with a "head back to your app" coaching cue); or the user re-enters a recording they had backgrounded, via the home "Recording" return pill. Dictation that stays in context never shows this surface: keyboard dictation while Jot is already foreground and voice-editing inside a transcript both record inline into the focused field, and the Action Button Shortcut and Warm-Hold keyboard dictation record in the background without presenting it.

Exception — keyboard dictation within the Warm Hold window: when a warm-hold session is still active, tapping Dictate in the keyboard does NOT bring Jot to the foreground. The recording starts in the background and the user remains in the host app; only the keyboard's streaming strip animates to reflect recording state. See §2.9 and §13.2 for details.
chunks.title: Full-Screen Recording Surface

chunks.text: Recording Status Indicator. Recording state is communicated implicitly — the dedicated full-screen surface and the live streaming transcript make it unmistakable that the microphone is active. The elapsed-time counter lives inside the blue stop button at the bottom of the screen as a monospace timer, so the duration of the session is always visible alongside the primary "stop" affordance rather than as a separate top-of-screen status line. During the external-keyboard cold-start withhold window (§2.1's exception case), the freed top space above the transcript carries quiet rotating micro-messages (e.g. "Recording stays on while you go," "looking away helps you find the words," "the thinking happens out loud, not on the screen"). Once the live stream reveals, or on an ordinary FAB-initiated recording, the freed top space instead shows a single fixed caption above the transcript ("A sharper transcriber takes a second pass when you stop and tidies the live text."), not a rotating pool.
chunks.title: Recording Status Indicator

chunks.text: Live Streaming Transcript. While the user speaks, a scrolling text area displays a continuously updating live preview of what is being said, rendered in an italic serif font. The preview is produced by the active dictation engine: Apple's engine (the default) streams it natively and firms it up in place as you talk, while Jot's own engine refreshes it by re-reading the most recent stretch of audio in sentence-sized chunks at natural pauses and every few seconds. Either way it is a rough running approximation, not the final text (see §2.8). The view auto-scrolls to follow the newest text so the user always sees the most recent words without manually scrolling. A soft fade at the top edge signals that more content exists above. Because the preview arrives in sentence-sized chunks (at speech pauses or every few seconds), the newest visible words can trail the voice by a few seconds — a quiet ellipsis sits right after the last word, its dots brightening in a slow cycle, signaling that transcription is still catching up and more text is on the way. With Reduce Motion enabled the ellipsis is a steady static one, and it disappears entirely while paused since nothing is being captured. The same trailing ellipsis appears in the keyboard's streaming strip. This live preview can be turned off with the "Live text while dictating" toggle in Settings → Dictation (on by default; turning it off saves battery and does not change the saved transcript; off by default on lower-memory iPhones) — the saved final transcript is unaffected (§2.8).
chunks.title: Live Streaming Transcript

chunks.text: Pause / Resume. A Pause control sits on the recording surface alongside Stop and Cancel. Pausing temporarily stops capturing audio without finalizing the recording — the session stays live and the same dictation continues when the user resumes, so the paused gap is simply absent from the saved audio. While paused, the recording dot goes static/hollow and the surface reads "Paused · mic ready, not capturing," and the elapsed timer freezes (it counts only time actually captured, so it resumes from where it left off). The microphone is kept warm during the pause for instant resume, which is why iOS keeps showing its orange microphone indicator — but nothing is captured or stored while paused, exactly as during Warm Hold; the on-screen wording makes the held-but-not-recording state explicit. The live streaming preview is preserved across a pause and new words append after resume rather than restarting. Only Resume or Stop / Cancel leave the paused state; a forgotten pause auto-finalizes once the session reaches the overall recording cap. Pause/Resume is available from both the recording surface and the Jot Keyboard.
chunks.title: Pause / Resume

chunks.text: Stop and Finalize. A large blue gradient stop button at the bottom of the screen ends the recording. The button contains a white stop square and the running elapsed-time monospace counter side-by-side. After stopping, a brief transcribing state is shown (the stop button displays a spinner) while the on-device speech model produces the final accurate transcript from the audio captured during the session — which may differ from the live preview shown during recording. Stop ends the recording from either the active or a paused state.
chunks.title: Stop and Finalize

chunks.text: Cancel Recording. A circular red trash-icon button at the trailing end of the bottom control row (alongside Pause/Resume and Stop) discards the current recording without saving any transcript, useful when the user dictated the wrong thing or changed their mind. It discards from either the active or a paused state.
chunks.title: Cancel Recording

chunks.text: Backgrounding the Recording Surface. The recording surface includes a visible back chevron at the top-left. Tapping it backgrounds the recording without cancelling it — for example, to glance at the home screen or another app — and the standard iOS edge-swipe-back gesture works the same way in parallel. The microphone and live transcription keep running; the home surface replaces the Dictate button with a blue "Recording" return pill that taps back into the live recording surface. Stopping or cancelling are the only ways to actually end a recording (see §2.5 and §2.6).
chunks.title: Backgrounding the Recording Surface

chunks.text: Live Preview & Final Transcript. How the live preview relates to the final saved transcript depends on the dictation engine. With Apple's engine (the default), the live preview streams natively as the user speaks and firms up in place; when the user stops, the transcript is finalized right away, so stopping stays fast even after a long dictation. With Jot's own engine, a single accurate model does both passes — there is no separate "fast" streaming model: while the user speaks it produces the live preview by repeatedly re-reading a trailing window of the recent audio (in sentence-sized chunks, at natural pauses and every few seconds), and when the user stops it re-reads the entire recording once more for the clean, fully-punctuated final. Either way the saved transcript can differ from — and reads better than — what scrolled by live, and it is always the version saved to the library. The live preview is the one part that can be switched off — via the "Live text while dictating" toggle in Settings → Dictation (and off by default on lower-memory iPhones) — without affecting the saved final transcript. On a fresh install or just after an update, Jot's own engine may still be loading for the first dictation; recording still begins the instant the user taps and nothing said is lost while it loads (see §2.14 and §2.9).
chunks.title: Live Preview & Final Transcript

chunks.text:
Auto-Dismiss on Completion. Once transcription finishes, the recording view dismisses itself automatically and the user lands on Jot's home view, with the new transcript already saved and available in the library.

When the dictation was initiated from a third-party app's keyboard (via the Jot down key) and there is no active Warm Hold session (cold start), Jot is brought to the foreground during recording and the user must manually swipe back to the host app — for example, by swiping right along the iOS app-switcher gesture bar. The transcribed text is pasted into the originating text field once the user returns to that app. Jot does not automatically switch the user back to the host app. On a fresh install or right after an update, the on-device speech model may still be loading when this cold start fires; in that case the recording begins capturing the instant the user taps — their voice is buffered while the model finishes loading, so nothing said during the wait is lost — and, only if the load is genuinely slow, the surface shows a short reassuring cold-start line (no progress bar) until the model is ready and the transcript catches up. Stopping before the model has finished simply waits for it, then transcribes the buffered audio.

Within the Warm Hold window, this flow is different: Jot is never brought to the foreground, so no manual swipe-back is needed. The keyboard's streaming strip shows recording progress in place, and when transcription completes the text is auto-pasted without the user leaving the host app. See §13.2 for the Warm Hold UI-path disclosure.
chunks.title: Auto-Dismiss on Completion

chunks.text: Automatic Clipboard Copy on Completion. When an in-app dictation — started from the home screen Dictate button or Recording Hero — finishes and the final transcript is saved, Jot automatically places the automatically cleaned transcript text on the system clipboard. The user can immediately paste it into any other app (Notes, Messages, Mail, a browser field, and so on) without any extra step: no need to open the transcript detail, tap a copy button, or long-press the row. This auto-copy happens as soon as the transcription completes — at the same moment the result becomes available to the Jot Keyboard — and precedes the Auto-Dismiss that returns the user to the library. The Action Button Shortcut similarly copies its result to the clipboard on completion; both flows share this behavior. Manual copy options — the row long-press, detail Copy button, and Actions Pane "Copy last" — remain available for later retrieval of any transcript.
chunks.title: Automatic Clipboard Copy on Completion

chunks.text:
Chained Follow-Up Voice Commands. Within 30 seconds after a dictation completes, the user can make a short follow-up dictation to transform the prior text — for example, "make it shorter" or "translate that to Spanish." Jot recognises this as a command against the just-dictated text rather than a new separate dictation: the transformed result replaces the prior text on the clipboard, a new transcript entry is created, and the original no longer appears in the keyboard's recent history. Outside the 30-second window, all new dictations are treated as fresh independent entries.

In the new entry's detail view, the command utterance itself (e.g., "make it shorter") becomes the Original tab text, while the transformed prior dictation appears under the Rewrite tab. This means a user opening the follow-up entry sees their voice command as the Original and the rewritten text — attributed as "Rewritten with [model name]" — as the Rewrite.

Home library vs. keyboard recents asymmetry: in the Home library, both the original transcript and the follow-up entry appear as separate rows — the original is not hidden or marked in any way. In the keyboard's recents strip, only the follow-up entry is shown; the original is filtered out and does not appear. A user browsing the Home library therefore sees the full chain, while a user glancing at the keyboard recents sees only the latest result.

See also: keyboard chained follow-up cross-reference.
chunks.title: Chained Follow-Up Voice Commands

chunks.text: Accessibility: VoiceOver Focus. When the recording surface opens via an automated entry path — such as a keyboard-initiated recording triggered by a deep link — VoiceOver focus is placed on the recording status element (pulsing dot and elapsed timer) so assistive technology users are immediately informed that recording is underway, rather than landing on the back-navigation button.
chunks.title: Accessibility: VoiceOver Focus

chunks.text:
Apple Watch Dictation. Jot ships a standalone Apple Watch app (watchOS 26+) for capturing thoughts directly from the watch — useful when reaching for the phone is awkward. Recording works without the iPhone present: audio is captured locally on the watch as a small compressed file and queued. Whenever the watch comes within range of the paired iPhone running Jot, queued recordings transfer automatically in the background and run through the same on-device transcription pipeline as in-app dictations — the resulting transcript appears in the Home library alongside everything else. The watch app is introduced to new users on the final Setup Wizard completion panel (W8), which surfaces a "one more thing" Apple Watch card.

Watch home screen. The screen opens directly on a large round blue "dictate" button that glows and slowly breathes — no app-name title, since you're already in the watch app. Tapping it starts recording; "Tap to dictate" sits just below. The page then scrolls into a "Recent" section: a header row with an "All N" link to the full list (shown once there are more than three transcripts), then any recordings still waiting on the phone shown at the top as "Waiting to sync" cards (a play button, the status, and how long ago it was captured in amber) — each disappears the moment the phone confirms receipt, with the finished transcript following seconds later. Tap a "Waiting to sync" card to play the recording back on the watch speaker (useful to hear, or to recover, one that's stuck), or swipe it left to delete it if you don't want to sync it. Below the pending cards sit the three most recent transcripts as tap-to-open cards. Recordings sync automatically, so there is no top-of-screen pending badge or success ribbon. At the very bottom — only reachable by scrolling past the transcripts — a single muted "Sync diagnostics ›" footer row leads to the connection-status surface and Reset sync button.

Recording sheet.
chunks.title: Apple Watch Dictation

chunks.text:
Below the pending cards sit the three most recent transcripts as tap-to-open cards. Recordings sync automatically, so there is no top-of-screen pending badge or success ribbon. At the very bottom — only reachable by scrolling past the transcripts — a single muted "Sync diagnostics ›" footer row leads to the connection-status surface and Reset sync button.

Recording sheet. Modal sheet centered on a large round coral button with the running mm:ss timer inside it — tapping the button stops and saves. The button carries no "Stop" word; a quiet "Tap to stop" hint sits below a live coral amplitude waveform. The button + waveform freeze (waveform replaced by a static "REC" cue) in Always-On Display and when Reduce Motion is enabled. The only outcome is a saved recording — there is no discard path: even dismissing the sheet saves the capture rather than losing it, so accidental taps can't lose audio. Recordings cap at 15 minutes per session; the watch warns at 14:30 with a haptic and banner so long captures aren't silently truncated. An extended runtime session keeps the recorder alive while the wrist is lowered.

Recent transcript list. The watch surfaces the most recent ten transcripts (read-only — taps open a full-text view; all editing happens on the phone). The top three appear inlined on the home screen as individual cards; the rest are one tap away via "All N". Watch-originated entries show a small watch glyph next to the date; transcripts captured on the phone show no glyph (the absence is the default). Recordings still waiting on the phone appear as "Waiting to sync" cards at the top of both lists — tap one to play it back, swipe left to delete it — and each clears as soon as the phone has it, with the real transcript following moments later. Opening a transcript shows its full text plus a "Synced to iPhone" confirmation row. A "Last synced" footer surfaces in amber on the full list if it's been more than 24 hours since the last successful sync.

Dictation language on the watch.
chunks.title: Apple Watch Dictation

chunks.text:
Recordings still waiting on the phone appear as "Waiting to sync" cards at the top of both lists — tap one to play it back, swipe left to delete it — and each clears as soon as the phone has it, with the real transcript following moments later. Opening a transcript shows its full text plus a "Synced to iPhone" confirmation row. A "Last synced" footer surfaces in amber on the full list if it's been more than 24 hours since the last successful sync.

Dictation language on the watch. Before recording, the user can scroll the Digital Crown to pick the dictation language from the same list available in Settings → Dictation → Language. The choice travels to the iPhone automatically, so when the queued recording is transcribed it uses the language selected on the watch — no separate step on the iPhone is needed. Most languages use Apple's on-device dictation on the iPhone and need nothing extra; the European languages only Jot's own engine can do require that iPhone to have already downloaded the one-time multilingual model (see §4.8 and §6.1). Like phone-captured dictations, a watch recording's source audio is retained on the iPhone for 3 days once it syncs, so it can be re-transcribed in another language within that window.

Complications + Smart Stack tile. A watch complication (corner, circular, inline variants) and a Smart Stack tile let the user start a recording in one tap from any watch face — both deep-link straight into the recording sheet.

Storage cap. The watch holds at most 50 pending recordings before new captures are blocked with an explicit alert ("Watch storage full — open Jot on iPhone to sync"). Fail-closed by design: silently dropping the oldest unsynced recording would be worse than the brief friction of forcing a sync.
chunks.title: Apple Watch Dictation

chunks.text: Cold-Start Loading. When a dictation starts while the speech model is still loading — typically the first dictation after an install or update, or after the system reclaimed the model's cache — recording begins capturing the instant the user taps (§2.9), so nothing said is lost. On a fast/warm load nothing special is shown beyond the normal "Listening…". Only a genuinely slow cold load surfaces a short reassuring line, and during a long load that line rotates through a few different messages so it doesn't sit static — there is no progress bar, no percentage, and no model name. This applies on both the recording surface and the keyboard streaming strip; the live transcript replaces it the moment the model is ready.
chunks.title: Cold-Start Loading

chunks.text: Dictation Engine. Jot transcribes with Apple's on-device dictation by default, for every language Apple supports on the device — English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese. It runs entirely on the iPhone or iPad, streams the live preview natively as you speak (see §2.8), and — because it's Apple's own engine — works on more devices: newer hardware uses Apple's newer, higher-accuracy dictation, and hardware too old for that automatically uses Apple's older but broadly-compatible dictation, so on-device dictation still works on devices where Jot's own engine can't run. Jot's own on-device engine (the more accurate one, historically Jot's only engine) is offered as an optional upgrade on the devices that can run it — iPhone 14 Pro and later, and iPad with M1 or later — through a one-time keyboard nudge that invites the user to switch to it for more precise English, keeping Apple's engine as a fallback. Anyone who was already using Jot before Apple's engine became the default keeps Jot's own engine after updating — the switch to an Apple default only changes what a brand-new install starts on. Jot's own engine is also the only engine for the European languages Apple can't do (Polish, Czech, Ukrainian, and others — see the Language picker), which download a one-time multilingual model. On devices that can't run Jot's own engine, Apple's dictation is simply used with no engine choice to make. Your custom vocabulary is applied on either engine (except for Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese, which Apple transcribes without the vocabulary pass). The engine choice is invisible in normal use — the recording surface and keyboard look and behave the same either way.
chunks.title: Dictation Engine

chunks.text: Original / Rewrite Tabs. The detail view for any transcript presents two tabs — Original and Rewrite — selectable via a two-pill segment control. The Original tab always shows the unmodified text produced by the speech model. The Rewrite tab shows the automatic cleanup output when present, and later shows the output of AI Rewrite if one has been generated; older entries with neither show an empty state with a prompt to create one. When cleanup or a rewrite already exists, the detail view defaults to the Rewrite tab on open so the improved text is immediately visible. A third Speakers tab appears alongside these two only when a multi-voice recording has been split into speaker turns — otherwise the segment control stays a two-pill (or single-tab) control.
chunks.title: Original / Rewrite Tabs

chunks.text: Transcript Metadata. A subline at the top of the detail view displays the relative recording date and the duration when available (present for live dictations; omitted for file transcriptions via Shortcuts), giving context without cluttering the reading area. A small language label appears in this subline alongside the existing provenance glyphs (such as the watch glyph for Apple Watch–originated entries) to indicate the language the transcript was dictated in — useful at a glance when the library contains notes in multiple languages. This recorded language is also used as the source for the Translate action and determines which language is offered for re-transcription. The detail view has no title surface — title and tag fields are intentionally absent from v1 (see also §7.11).
chunks.title: Transcript Metadata

chunks.text: Selectable Text. Both the original transcript text and the rewrite text are fully selectable, allowing users to copy any portion to the clipboard using the standard iOS text selection handles. On devices with Apple Intelligence, selecting the text also surfaces the system Writing Tools (Rewrite, Make Concise, Proofread, and more) — which Jot points users to when its own rewrite model isn't downloaded.
chunks.title: Selectable Text

chunks.text: Rewrite Attribution. When a rewrite is present, a small attribution line names the active rewrite model. The label always reflects whichever rewrite model is currently selected in Settings; the UI does not distinguish between automatic cleanup output and downloaded-model output. The attribution row also hosts the rewrite feedback affordance (thumbs up / thumbs down) and the Discard rewrite button.
chunks.title: Rewrite Attribution

chunks.text: Rewrite Feedback. The Rewrite Attribution row hosts a 👍 / 👎 pair to the left of the Discard button. Tapping one sets the rating; tapping the active glyph again clears it; tapping the opposite glyph swaps it. A light haptic confirms each tap and the glyph fills in (hand.thumbsup.fill in accent blue or hand.thumbsdown.fill in red) when active. The rating is local and private; nothing is uploaded. It pairs with the Edit Rewrite flow to produce a complete signal — a 👎 plus a user correction is the strongest data for future model fine-tuning, but each half is meaningful on its own (a 👎 with no edit still says "this was wrong but I didn't have time"; a 👍 with no edit says "the model nailed it"). The rating clears whenever the underlying rewrite changes — tapping Rewrite regenerates the rewrite and resets the rating; Discard clears the rewrite, edit, and rating together (see §13.5).
chunks.title: Rewrite Feedback

chunks.text: Action Bar. A row of actions at the bottom of the detail view provides five actions, left-to-right: Delete, Edit, a Rewrite control (an accent sparkle circle that opens the rewrite Prompt Picker), a Translate globe (opens the on-device Translate sheet for the active tab directly), and Copy. The earlier full-width "Rewrite" pill was replaced by the compact sparkle circle so it no longer dominates the bar — which also reads cleanly when the Apple Intelligence rewrite engine is selected and the control simply points to the system Writing Tools. Delete sits on the far-left so the destructive action is harder to hit accidentally; Copy sits on the far-right where the right-hand thumb naturally falls. The Copy button is icon-only — there is no visible text label. After tapping Copy, the icon changes to a checkmark briefly before reverting to the copy icon after approximately 1.3 seconds, confirming the action to the user. The VoiceOver accessibility label updates from "Copy transcript" to "Copied to clipboard" during this window. Tapping Delete shows a confirmation dialog before the entry is permanently removed. When the entry has no AI Rewrite, it reads "Delete this entry?" with a destructive "Delete" button and a "Cancel" button. When a rewrite exists, it instead reads "Delete this entry or just the rewrite?" with three options: "Delete this entry" (destructive), "Delete rewrite only" (destructive, discards just the rewrite and keeps the original), and "Cancel".
chunks.title: Action Bar

chunks.text: Rewrite Progress and Cancellation. When a rewrite is actively running, a progress card appears alongside the action bar (the action bar itself remains visible) with a "Rewriting…" indicator and a Cancel button, allowing the user to abort the generation mid-stream.
chunks.title: Rewrite Progress and Cancellation

chunks.text: Edit Transcript. The Edit pencil in the action bar turns the currently-visible tab into an editable text field with a slim bottom bar offering Cancel and a blue Save (✓) button. The tab pill is hidden while editing — one tab at a time. Editing the Original tab overwrites the transcript text in place; the pre-edit speech-model output is not retained (the user's correction becomes the new ground truth). Editing the Rewrite tab keeps the model's rewrite frozen as the "before" and saves the user's correction as the "after," so the pair is preserved as a future-improvement training signal (see §13.5). Tapping Rewrite after an edit generates a fresh rewrite and clears the prior user-edit; tapping the Rewrite tab's Discard affordance clears both the model rewrite and any user edit together. The Edit pill is disabled while a rewrite is mid-flight and while the back chevron is also disabled mid-edit so accidental swipes don't silently lose work. While editing, dictating into the field works the same way as any other focused field in Jot: tap Dictate on the system or Jot keyboard, and the transcribed text is inserted at the cursor when the keyboard's recording stops — there is no separate in-editor microphone control. While editing, any text the user adds or changes during this session — whether typed or dictated — is shown in *italic*, while the untouched original text stays upright, so it's easy to see exactly what was changed. The italic is a live editing cue only: on Save everything is stored as plain text and the next time the entry is opened it all reads upright again. Edit mode also offers Find & Replace for fixing a repeatedly-misheard word in one pass.
chunks.title: Edit Transcript

chunks.text: Translate. The Rewrite Prompt Picker includes a Translate option that opens a lightweight translate sheet. The source is the transcript’s own recorded language (visible as the language badge in the subline); the user picks a target language from a row of chips — all supported languages including English — with the transcript’s own language excluded from the list. The active tab’s text — whether the Original or the Rewrite — is translated instantly, shown as a serif quote with Copy and Share actions. Translation is read-once: it is not saved to the transcript, does not occupy the Rewrite tab, and leaves both the original and any rewrite untouched. It runs entirely on this iPhone using the system’s built-in translation (offline after a one-time per-language download the system manages), so the text never leaves the device (§13.1). It is distinct from the optional “Translate to…” rewrite-prompt template, which runs through the on-device rewrite model and *saves* into the Rewrite tab — this Translate option is faster, needs no model download, and is ephemeral. See also §3.11 for the related option to re-run transcription in a different language while the source audio is still retained.
chunks.title: Translate

chunks.text: Find & Replace (while editing). While editing a transcript, a magnifying-glass button in the edit bar opens a Find & Replace bar above the keyboard — for when the speech model misheard the same word several times. The user types a word to find (whole-word, case-insensitive matches are counted live) and a replacement, then taps Replace All to fix every occurrence at once; the changed words show in *italic* like any other edit until Save. Find & Replace operates on whichever tab is being edited (Original or Rewrite) and is available only in edit mode. When a replacement looks like a genuine term correction — a one- or two-word term that isn't an everyday word, swapped in two or more places — Save shows a gentle one-tap offer to add the corrected term to your vocabulary: it adds the term, remembers the misheard form as a "sounds-like" so the keyboard's correction prompts can catch it, and teaches the system so the next dictation gets it right by itself (the same path as selecting a word and choosing Add to Vocabulary). The offer is dismissible and never blocks; declining changes nothing.
chunks.title: Find & Replace (while editing)

chunks.text: Source Audio Retention & Re-Transcribe. Jot keeps the source audio of every recording on-device for 3 days — silently and automatically, and never leaving the device (§13.1). The 3-day window is measured from when the audio enters Jot, not from when it was originally spoken: for a live dictation that is the moment the recording finishes, and for a file shared into Jot from another app it is the moment the import completes — so a shared clip always gets its full 3 days on-device regardless of how old the file was. Within that window, a re-transcribe affordance appears in the transcript detail subline (the same area as the language badge): the user picks a language and Jot re-runs the speech model on the original audio, replacing the transcript text with the new result. This is useful when, for example, a note was dictated in English before the multilingual model was downloaded, and the user wants to switch the transcription to a European language — they download the model (see §6.1 and §4.8), then re-transcribe while the audio is still retained. After 3 days the audio is deleted automatically (no manual step needed) and the re-transcribe affordance disappears; the saved transcript text is unaffected. The retained audio is excluded from iCloud Backup and is stored only locally. Re-transcription produces a new language badge reflecting the chosen language and acts as the new source for Translate. While the audio is still retained, it is also what Detect speakers runs on.
chunks.title: Source Audio Retention & Re-Transcribe

chunks.text: Speaker Notes. When a recording has more than one voice, Jot can split its transcript into per-speaker turns. On any transcript whose source audio is still retained, a Detect speakers action lives in the detail overflow menu — the same ⋯ menu as Re-transcribe — and runs an on-device pass that groups the audio by who is talking. If it finds more than one speaker, the detail view gains a third Speakers tab beside Original and Rewrite, listing each turn with its speaker label, its time range, and its text (selectable like the rest of the transcript). Turns spoken by the phone's owner are labeled "You" — Jot learns the owner's voice automatically from their own past solo recordings, with no enrollment step — and other voices are "Speaker 1", "Speaker 2", and so on in the order they first speak; until Jot has heard enough of the owner's voice every turn is anonymous, and the feature still works. Audio shared into Jot from another app (for example a call recording) is checked for multiple speakers automatically right after it is transcribed, so a multi-voice import arrives already carrying its Speakers tab; a single-voice note changes nothing, and speaker detection never blocks, delays, or fails an import — if it can't run, the transcript is saved exactly as it would be otherwise. Because the saved turns hold the transcript text exactly as it read at detection time, editing the Original text or re-transcribing the audio clears the Speakers tab (you can run Detect speakers again while the audio is still retained). Speaker detection runs entirely on this iPhone (§13.1); it uses a small extra model that Jot fetches quietly over Wi-Fi so it is ready when needed, and downloads on demand otherwise.
chunks.title: Speaker Notes

chunks.text: Welcome (W1). The first wizard panel introduces Jot with a large wordmark headline and a short tagline, then offers a single "Get started" call-to-action that begins the setup flow. W1 also has the standard wizard close (X) button with a "Skip setup?" confirmation prompt (same as on every other panel).
chunks.title: Welcome (W1)

chunks.text: Microphone Permission (W3). The microphone-permission panel requests microphone access via the system permission dialog. If the user grants permission, the wizard advances automatically. If permission was previously denied, the panel shows a deep-link button that opens iOS Settings directly to Jot's permission page so the user can enable it without hunting through menus.
chunks.title: Microphone Permission (W3)

chunks.text: Keyboard Installation & Full Access (W4). The keyboard-installation panel sends users to Keyboard Settings once to add Jot and turn on Full Access. When the keyboard has not been detected, the panel title reads "Add the Jot keyboard" and the primary call-to-action reads "Open Settings"; when the user returns with Jot installed, the title updates to "Keyboard ready" and the button changes to "Continue." Jot can detect keyboard installation via the system's installed-keyboards list, but it cannot detect Full Access directly — Full Access remains a manual user attestation. A secondary "I've already added it" button is shown only in the not-yet-detected state as an escape hatch; once the keyboard is detected, "Continue" is the only footer action. See §13.3.
chunks.title: Keyboard Installation & Full Access (W4)

chunks.text: How It Works (W5). The how-it-works panel is a looping animated mini-phone illustration cycling through four numbered steps — "Tap Jot down on your keyboard," "Jot opens and starts recording," "Swipe back to your app," "Stop from the keyboard when you're done" — each highlighted in sync in a step list below the animation as it plays. An honest footnote above the "Got it" button explains the app-switch: iOS doesn't let keyboards use the mic directly, so Jot hops to the foreground to capture; if that ever changes, the hop goes away. Honors Reduce Motion (the animation freezes on its final frame). This orientation screen has no required user action other than reading and tapping "Got it". This same animated scene is reused on the Help → How Jot Works page.
chunks.title: How It Works (W5)

chunks.text: Keyboard Try-It (W6). The keyboard try-it panel is a guided "try the keyboard" step. The user taps a practice field, which raises the keyboard; if the system keyboard appears instead of Jot, an in-field cue tells them to tap the globe key to switch to the Jot keyboard (escalating to "it's the bottom-left key" if they linger). They tap "Jot down", their words stream live in the keyboard, and on stop the result is pasted into the practice field as an "it works" moment, following the normal automatic cleanup path. The user then taps Continue themselves — the panel does not auto-advance — and a manual "I tried it" button allows skipping. By the time the user reaches this panel the speech model is usually ready, so the dictation starts without a wait; on a fresh install where it is still loading, the same cold-start line appears briefly and the result still arrives. This is the wizard's only "try it" step — practicing inside the wizard surface was dropped so users experience Jot exactly as they will use it after setup.
chunks.title: Keyboard Try-It (W6)

chunks.text: Warm Hold Opt-In (W7). The warm-hold panel offers the Warm Hold feature: keeping the microphone session alive for 2 minutes after each recording to reduce startup latency for the next dictation. The user flips a "Keep mic ready" toggle (showing an "Always" / "Off" status) and taps Continue; the choice is saved to Settings and can be changed later via Settings → Privacy, where the duration is also customizable (60s, 2 min, 3 min, or 5 min).
chunks.title: Warm Hold Opt-In (W7)

chunks.text: Completion (W8). The eighth and final panel congratulates the user with a "You're ready." headline and a body line ("Jot works now — start dictating in any app, any time."), then closes onboarding with a single "Start jotting." call-to-action. There is no longer a fork to an optional AI Rewrite step — AI Rewrite is set up later from Settings → AI whenever the user wants it, not during onboarding. Below the body, W8 shows a "one more thing" Apple Watch card — a soft-blue tile with a watch glyph, the title "It's on your wrist, too," and a line noting that ideas captured on the watch sync back automatically — introducing the Apple Watch app before the user finishes setup.
chunks.title: Completion (W8)

chunks.text: Dictation Language Picker (W2). The language-selection panel is the second wizard step — it appears immediately after the Welcome screen, before the Microphone Permission step. The list shows only the languages that actually work on this device, and never offers a download that couldn't run here. English is selected by default and needs no download. Many common languages — Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese — are handled by Apple's on-device dictation and also need no download. Choosing one of the additional European languages that only Jot's own engine can do (Polish, Czech, Ukrainian, and others) triggers a one-time multilingual model download (~461 MB); the panel shows download progress in place and advances to a "Ready" state when complete, unlocking every such language at once so future switches among them cost nothing extra. The searchable language list keeps a Recent section pinned at the top — the active language followed by the ones most recently used (up to five) — so switching among a handful of languages doesn't mean scrolling the full list each time; the recents are shared with the Settings language picker. The selection is saved and can be changed later from Settings → Dictation → Language; on the Apple Watch the Digital Crown serves the same language-selection role. Choosing a language here is the first step toward re-transcribing a note in a different language.
chunks.title: Dictation Language Picker (W2)

chunks.text: Wizard Navigation Chrome. Every wizard panel except Welcome (W1) shares a consistent chrome: a back chevron (top-left) that steps to the previous panel, and a close button (top-right, X) that exits the wizard entirely. Welcome has no previous step, so the back chevron is absent on that panel. Tapping the close button shows a "Skip setup?" confirmation dialog before dismissing. If a recording is in progress when the wizard is exited, the recording is stopped automatically so no audio is left capturing in the background. A left-edge swipe gesture (drag rightward from the leading 22 pt strip) performs the same back action as the back chevron.
chunks.title: Wizard Navigation Chrome

chunks.text: Wizard Progress Dots. At the top of every wizard panel, a row of eight dots represents the eight setup steps. The current step's dot is larger and filled in the accent color; completed steps are smaller filled dots; upcoming steps are smaller outlined dots.
chunks.title: Wizard Progress Dots

chunks.text: Dictation-Only Design. Jot's keyboard is dictation-only and has no QWERTY layout. Users keep their regular system keyboard for typing and switch to Jot only to dictate. This is surfaced explicitly in the How It Works wizard step so users understand the intended workflow before completing setup.
chunks.title: Dictation-Only Design

chunks.text: Full Custom Keyboard. Jot replaces the system keyboard with a fully custom layout when active. The layout is recording-controls-first: a top information strip and an action row with the primary controls — Pause + Stop + Cancel, with Cancel rendered as a trash-can on the left for easy reach — plus a single adaptive Enter key whose glyph adapts to the host field's return action (return-arrow, search glyph, Go, or Send). On wider devices the controls and Enter sit in one line; on narrower devices the layout adapts and keeps Enter on its own row below. The keyboard uses native side margins so it does not span the full screen width, sits at a fixed height, and styles itself to match the host app's light or dark appearance automatically. Below it, Apple's fixed system row (globe / dictation) remains. See §5.4 Dictate / Stop and §5.8 Pause / Resume.
chunks.title: Full Custom Keyboard

chunks.text: Recents Strip (Idle State). When the keyboard is idle (not recording), the top strip shows up to ten recent dictation entries with their timestamps and truncated cleaned text. Each row is split into two tappable zones: the body (timestamp + text) re-inserts that transcript at the cursor, and a small trailing button (arrow.up.forward.app glyph, accent color) brings the main app to the foreground and opens that transcript's detail view (§3) — useful for reviewing, running a Rewrite, or sharing without leaving the keyboard's host app to find the entry manually. The strip is scrollable, with a soft fade at the bottom edge indicating additional entries below. Entries that have an AI Rewrite display a small coral sparkles glyph inside the body zone before the trailing button — the same affordance used in the home library so the visual language stays consistent across surfaces. A "See all" link brings the main app to the foreground via a deep link. If the app is on the home screen with no overlays active, the transcript library is visible; the deep link does not force a navigation reset, so if a sheet or other navigation is already open the user will not automatically land on the library. Full Access is required for the recents strip to show any content: without it, the entire strip is replaced by an instructional card ("Enable Full Access to Dictate") with a lock-shield icon and the two-step path to turn it on (iPhone Settings → General → Keyboard, then Keyboards → Jot Keyboard → Allow Full Access) (see §5.11). While a row is held, it lights with a subtle blue highlight and a thin leading accent bar so the user can see exactly which entry their touch is on, and a small contextual hint appears in the strip header naming the action — "Pastes here" while pressing a row body, "Opens in Jot" while pressing the trailing button. This is purely visual feedback layered on the existing gestures: a tap still pastes, and pressing then scrolling still scrolls the list without pasting, exactly as before.
chunks.title: Recents Strip (Idle State)

chunks.text:
While a row is held, it lights with a subtle blue highlight and a thin leading accent bar so the user can see exactly which entry their touch is on, and a small contextual hint appears in the strip header naming the action — "Pastes here" while pressing a row body, "Opens in Jot" while pressing the trailing button. This is purely visual feedback layered on the existing gestures: a tap still pastes, and pressing then scrolling still scrolls the list without pasting, exactly as before.

### 5.2a Warm-Hold Switching Nudge
After the user has bounced between another app and the keyboard to dictate a few times in a row, the top strip can temporarily show a nudge card in place of the recents strip: "Bouncing back and forth to dictate? Keep the mic ready so the next one starts instantly." with two actions — "Keep mic ready" (turns on Warm Hold) and "Don't show this again" (dismisses the suggestion for good). It only appears for users who haven't already enabled Warm Hold, and never interrupts an in-progress dictation.

### 5.2b More-Accurate-Engine Upgrade Nudge
On devices that can run Jot's own dictation engine (iPhone 14 Pro and later, iPad M1 and later), after the user has dictated in English a handful of times on Apple's default engine, the keyboard's top strip can show a one-time nudge card in place of the recents strip: "More accurate dictation available." / "Switch to Jot's own on-device engine." with two actions — Switch (opens a short sheet in the main app that explains Jot's own engine is more precise for English and runs fully on-device, with Apple's engine kept as a fallback; confirming there switches English dictation to Jot's engine) and Not now (dismisses the suggestion for good). It is a twin of the Warm-Hold switching nudge — same card style, never shown at the same time as it, and never interrupting an in-progress dictation. It appears only once; either declining or switching retires it for good. This nudge and its sheet are the user-facing way to move off Apple's default engine (see §2.15).
chunks.title: Recents Strip (Idle State)

chunks.text: Streaming Strip (Recording State). When a dictation is in progress inside the keyboard, the top strip transforms into a live recording display: a blue pulsing dot, an elapsed timer, a six-bar animated waveform, a brief header status line ("We tidy this up when you stop") noting the live text gets a cleanup pass once recording ends, and a scrollable pane that shows the live preview transcript in real time, rendered in the same small italic serif used by the recording surface. This live preview honours the same "Live text while dictating" setting as the recording surface; with it off the pane stays empty and only the final transcript pastes on stop. When a cold start begins before the speech model has finished loading, the pane shows the same cold-start loading treatment in place of the partial text — a short reassuring line (no progress bar) only if the load is genuinely slow — and switches to the live transcript the moment the model is ready (recording is already capturing the whole time, so nothing said during the load is lost). The pane is bottom-anchored — the first words appear near the bottom of the pane and older lines push upward as more text arrives — with the same trailing "still transcribing" ellipsis as the recording surface's live preview (quiet accent-blue dots right after the newest word, brightening in a slow cycle; static under Reduce Motion) and a top-edge fade for overflow; the visible stream is capped to a bounded height so it never grows past the strip. While the dictation is paused, the pulsing dot goes static/hollow, the timer freezes, "Paused · mic ready, not capturing" is shown, and the waveform hides; the partial text already shown is kept (its trailing ellipsis hidden, since nothing is being captured) and resuming appends to it. A "↓ live" pill appears when the user has manually scrolled up and the view is no longer tracking the newest content; tapping the pill restores auto-follow.
chunks.title: Streaming Strip (Recording State)

chunks.text: While the dictation is paused, the pulsing dot goes static/hollow, the timer freezes, "Paused · mic ready, not capturing" is shown, and the waveform hides; the partial text already shown is kept (its trailing ellipsis hidden, since nothing is being captured) and resuming appends to it. A "↓ live" pill appears when the user has manually scrolled up and the view is no longer tracking the newest content; tapping the pill restores auto-follow. Follow-up voice commands (see §2.11) apply within the 30-second window after the keyboard dictation completes.
chunks.title: Streaming Strip (Recording State)

chunks.text: Dictate / Stop Control. A prominent pill button in the keyboard's action row toggles recording on and off. The label and appearance change to reflect the current state — "Dictate" when idle, active stop styling when recording — so the current state is always unambiguous. While recording it is joined by Pause / Resume and a trash-can Cancel on the left (§5.1). When Full Access is not enabled, the button displays "Enable Full Access" and tapping it opens Jot's iOS Settings page (from which the user navigates to Keyboards → Jot to toggle Full Access) instead of starting a recording.
chunks.title: Dictate / Stop Control

chunks.text: Post-Stop "Working" State. Immediately after the user stops a keyboard dictation, the Jot down button transitions to a "Working" label while transcription finishes on-device. The keyboard remains visible and the user can see that processing is in progress before the result is inserted. If Jot has a candidate correction to the user's custom vocabulary, the keyboard normally holds the paste and shows a small review card asking the user to answer one question (e.g. "what should this say?") before the text is inserted at all — see §8.8 Vocabulary Correction Prompts in the Keyboard. Only in the rare case where the candidate correction isn't ready in time (a late-arriving check that lost the race with the paste) does the review instead appear as a post-paste teaching card after the result has already landed.
chunks.title: Post-Stop "Working" State

chunks.text: Actions Pane. The ••• actions button opens a full-width actions pane in the keyboard's top region (in place of the recents strip, never overlaying the controls), laid out as a grid of tiles. Feature tiles: Add to Vocabulary — adds the host's currently-selected word to the Vocabulary term list (enabled only with a selection); AI Rewrite and Translate — short guides (nothing runs in the keyboard) that teach iOS's own selection-menu tools, showing the actual menu glyph to tap rather than just naming it, with the headings set in the app's serif display face. Edit tiles: Copy, Paste, and Undo / Redo — Undo/Redo work off a stack (up to 20 steps) and each shows a count badge of how many steps remain that way; tapping Undo moves one step to the redo side and vice-versa, so the badges always reflect what's available. A Close tile dismisses the pane (tapping ••• again also closes it). Results of these actions surface in the status banner.
chunks.title: Actions Pane

chunks.text: Backspace. The backspace key deletes one character per tap. There is currently no hold-to-repeat behavior.
chunks.title: Backspace

chunks.text: Pause / Resume. While a keyboard dictation is in progress, a Pause control sits in the action row next to Stop and the trash-can Cancel (§5.1). It is the same Pause / Resume behavior as the recording surface: pausing keeps the microphone warm and the dictation open without finalizing it, the streaming strip shows "Paused · mic ready, not capturing" with a static dot and frozen timer, and resuming continues the same dictation with new words appended. Pause can be initiated and cleared from the keyboard without bringing the main app to the foreground; the paused/resumed state stays in sync between the keyboard and the recording surface.
chunks.title: Pause / Resume

chunks.text: Dark / Light Mode Adaptation. The keyboard reads the host app's keyboard appearance setting and renders itself accordingly, so Jot's keyboard matches dark-mode apps natively without any user configuration. The rest of the app adapts to the system appearance the same way — see §1.13.
chunks.title: Dark / Light Mode Adaptation

chunks.text:
Full Access Requirement. The return key works without Full Access. Backspace and Undo/Redo also work without Full Access. The following actions are specifically gated:

- Jot down: when Full Access is absent, the Jot down button is replaced by an "Enable Full Access" CTA (with a lock-shield icon). Tapping it opens iOS Settings to Jot's app-settings page; from there the user navigates General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Jot Keyboard → Allow Full Access to flip the toggle.
- Paste: the Paste row in the Actions Pane stays visually enabled and tappable without Full Access (it is never dimmed), but tapping it silently does nothing, because clipboard reads are unavailable. No error is shown.
- Copy: the Copy row in the Actions Pane is silently disabled without Full Access, because the keyboard can only read the host's selected text when Full Access is granted. No error is shown.
- Status banner: the banner that relays dictation result messages is suppressed entirely when Full Access is absent.
- Recents strip content: without Full Access the entire strip is replaced by an instructional card guiding the user to enable it (see §5.2) — there is no "See all" link to tap in this state, since the strip itself isn't shown.

The Setup Wizard guides users through enabling Full Access during initial setup. See also §6.4 Privacy Controls for the Full Access informational row in Settings and §13.3 Full Access Disclosure for the canonical explanation of why Full Access is required.
chunks.title: Full Access Requirement

chunks.text: Auto-Paste of Completed Dictation. When a keyboard dictation finishes and the transcript is ready, the keyboard automatically inserts the automatically cleaned text into the host app's focused text field — no tap required. This is the core workflow the How It Works wizard step illustrates: speak, stop, and the text appears at the cursor. The auto-paste arms at the moment the user taps Stop and fires as soon as the final transcript is available.
chunks.title: Auto-Paste of Completed Dictation

chunks.text:
Speech Model Management. Jot chooses the dictation engine and any speech model automatically, based on the language and the device — there is no engine selector or variant picker in normal use. Most languages are transcribed by Apple's on-device dictation, which needs no download and is available immediately on install, so the first dictation works offline. The European languages Apple can't do use Jot's own engine with a separate multilingual model downloaded once on first selection. Jot's own engine is also offered as an optional English accuracy upgrade on capable devices (iPhone 14 Pro and later, iPad M1 and later) through the keyboard nudge — there is no engine toggle to hunt for here. Because none of this is something the user manages, the Settings card is labelled "Dictation" and carries only two controls — no model name, no readiness pill, no engine picker, and no "runs entirely on this iPhone" footer:

- Language — a picker for the dictation language. It lists only the languages that work on this device and never offers a download that can't run here. English and the other Apple-supported languages are available with no download. Choosing one of the European languages that only Jot's own engine can do triggers a one-time multilingual model download (~461 MB); once downloaded, every such language is unlocked and switching among them is free. The picker menu keeps a Recent section at the top — the active language plus the ones most recently used (up to five, shared with the wizard language picker) — for quick switching without scrolling the full list. The same language choice is made during the first-run Setup Wizard language step. On the Apple Watch, the Digital Crown sets the language on the watch side and the choice syncs to the iPhone. The selected language is recorded with each transcript (visible as a language badge in Transcript Detail) and used as the source for Translate. Any transcript's source audio can be re-transcribed in a different language.
chunks.title: Speech Model Management

chunks.text:
On the Apple Watch, the Digital Crown sets the language on the watch side and the choice syncs to the iPhone. The selected language is recorded with each transcript (visible as a language badge in Transcript Detail) and used as the source for Translate. Any transcript's source audio can be re-transcribed in a different language.
- Live text while dictating — a toggle (on by default) that controls whether the live preview is shown while recording. Turning it off saves battery and does not change the saved transcript; it starts off by default on lower-memory iPhones.

Vocabulary Boost applies on either engine (except for Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese — see §2.15), regardless of these settings.
chunks.title: Speech Model Management

chunks.text: Vocabulary Settings Link. A row shows the current count of custom vocabulary terms and navigates to the full Vocabulary settings screen where terms can be managed.
chunks.title: Vocabulary Settings Link

chunks.text: AI Settings Link. A row in the AI section shows the current status of the AI Rewrite model and navigates to the full AI Rewrite settings screen where the model can be downloaded, freed, and prompts can be managed. The screen opens with a rewrite-engine choice — Apple Intelligence (the device's built-in Writing Tools; the default when the device supports it, with no download) or Jot's AI (the downloadable Qwen model). Choosing Apple Intelligence hides the saved-prompt list and shows a short how-to instead (Writing Tools don't use Jot's prompts); choosing Jot's AI shows the model status and the user's prompts. Switching to Apple Intelligence is also how a user turns the downloaded model off and frees its space (see §7.10). There is no longer a choice of which model answers Ask Jot — Ask always uses Apple Intelligence, so the former "Use on-board Qwen for Ask" toggle has been removed (see §14.5).
chunks.title: AI Settings Link

chunks.text: Privacy Controls. A Privacy section shows a tappable Full Access row (subline "General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Jot", trailing external-arrow), plus a toggle for Warm Hold after wizard step W7. When Warm Hold is on, the toggle is followed by a "Ready for" duration picker with 60s, 2 min, 3 min, and 5 min options. The Full Access row opens iOS Settings to Jot's app-settings page; the subline gives the user the breadcrumb to navigate from there to Allow Full Access (Jot cannot read its state directly — see §13.3). The bottom-of-section caption "Your words stay on your iPhone. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry — only feedback you send is ever transmitted." carries the on-device-only message (with Send Feedback named as the sole exception); no separate "On-device only" row is shown. The matching "Your privacy is protected" explainer is shown on the iOS system-Settings page for Jot, not as a row here (see §13.6a).
chunks.title: Privacy Controls

chunks.text: About & Support. An About section provides links to Help & Support (opens Help), an Apple Watch row (opens a screen showing watch connection status with a Reset sync button — see §2.13), Re-run setup wizard (restarts the Setup Wizard from the beginning for troubleshooting or exploration), Send feedback (opens an in-app feedback form — see §9.6), the app version number, Donations (opens the in-app Donations screen), Jot for Mac (opens the Jot for Mac screen), a Privacy Policy link, an Acknowledgements screen (see §6.6), and a Diagnostics screen — a scrollable on-device log of recent app events (recording start/stop, paste outcomes, the vocabulary gate's decisions) that can be copied or cleared, surfaced for troubleshooting and containing no personal data (relocated here from the Help screen). When at least one dictation has been recorded, a "Time saved" row appears as the first entry of the About card, showing minutes saved today, the cumulative dictation count, and a small 14-day blue sparkline — the same lifetime stats that the home page used to surface inline, relocated here so the home view stays focused on recent activity (see §1.1).
chunks.title: About & Support

chunks.text: Acknowledgements. A dedicated Acknowledgements screen credits the open-source software and open-weight models that Jot is built on. It is organised into two sections: "Models & fonts" — listing the on-device speech models, the AI rewrite model (Qwen 3.5 4B), and the typeface used in the app, each with the author, license type, and a tappable link to the upstream source — and "Swift packages" — listing the major third-party Swift packages used by the app, with attribution and source links. Note: the list is curated and may not include every package the app uses. A footer note reiterates that all speech recognition and AI rewriting runs on-device and that no audio or transcript data is shared with any of the credited parties.
chunks.title: Acknowledgements

chunks.text:
Donations. The Donations screen is reached from Settings → About as an in-app navigation push. It explains Jot's free model, optionally personalizes the message with the user's estimated time saved when they have dictated for at least five minutes, and shows a searchable list of charities with their current Jot-raised totals. Live totals, donation counts, and the community total come from Jot's donations summary feed; each charity's one-line description (and logo, where available) comes from Jot's charity metadata file and is merged in by charity. Each charity row offers $2 and $10 quick-give actions that open the matching Every.org donation page in the system browser. If current totals cannot be refreshed, the screen shows the last known totals when available, or a retry state when no totals have ever loaded.

A gentle donation prompt also appears on the home screen as a centered popup once the user has built up meaningful usage — gated on cumulative dictation time and a one-week grace after first use so brand-new users are never asked on day one. It re-appears at increasing usage milestones rather than only once: choosing "Not now" simply defers it to the next milestone. The prompt offers "See donations" (opens the donations page) or "Not now", and never blocks dictation. The usage totals that drive it persist across app updates. The same cumulative usage total also drives the one-time Jot for Mac home prompt, shown in the same popup style.
chunks.title: Donations

chunks.text:
Your Data (Export & Import). *Currently hidden behind a flag — not reachable in the shipped app; the feature below is fully built but switched off pending a decision to re-expose it.*

A Your Data area in Settings lets the user export all their transcripts to a file and import them back. Export produces a single file containing every transcript (Original and Rewrite text); the user can save it to Files, share it, or send it anywhere they can keep a file. Import reads such a file and merges the transcripts into the library — the operation is idempotent: re-importing a file that contains entries already on the device never creates duplicates, so it is safe to import the same export more than once. This is an on-device backup and restore safety net for the transcript library, independent of iCloud Backup (see §13.4 for what iCloud Device Backup does and does not include) — it works on devices without iCloud, and the user controls the file. It does not export AI Rewrite prompts, vocabulary terms, or app preferences — only transcript content.
chunks.title: Your Data (Export & Import)

chunks.text:
Jot for Mac. A permanent "Jot for Mac" row in Settings → About opens a dedicated screen pitching the Mac app (same on-device dictation, on a bigger screen). The screen shows the download site's address, a "Send to your Mac" button that opens the system share sheet with the download link — the easiest way to hand it to another device, whether that's AirDropping it straight to the Mac or messaging/emailing the link to yourself — and an "Open jot-transcribe.com" button that opens the site directly in Safari.

Separately, a one-time home-screen prompt — "Jot is on your Mac too" — appears once after the user has built up about an hour of cumulative dictation time, in the same centered-popup style as the donation prompt. Unlike the donation prompt it never re-appears: choosing "Get Jot for Mac" or "Not now" both permanently retire it, since there's only one Mac app to point at. "Get Jot for Mac" opens the same Jot for Mac screen described above.
chunks.title: Jot for Mac

chunks.text: Automatic Cleanup. Jot strips the most obvious filler tokens — "um", "uh", "er", "uhm", "erm" and their elongated variants — from every dictation before it lands on the clipboard or in the library. This is a fast lexical sweep that always runs: there is no toggle, no separate model, no extra download, and nothing leaves the device. The cleaned text is what appears in the Original transcript surface, gets pasted into the host app, and is what AI Rewrite operates on when invoked. Paragraph boundaries inserted by the segmenter are preserved (the sweep only consumes adjacent spaces, never newlines), and obvious words containing filler-like substrings ("umbrella", "umpire", etc.) are left intact because the sweep is anchored on word boundaries. When the user dictates again right after a previous dictation, Jot inserts a separating space ahead of the new text so consecutive dictations don't run together into one unbroken sentence. The legacy "Clean Up Transcript" parameter on the "Transcribe Audio with Jot" Shortcuts action is a separate per-run flag that uses Apple Intelligence and continues to default to off.
chunks.title: Automatic Cleanup

chunks.text: On-Device AI Rewrite Model. Jot offers an optional on-device language model download that enables a full prose rewrite of any transcript. The model runs entirely on-device with no data sent to any server. Fresh installs default to the current rewrite model (about 2.5 GB on disk); the Switch Model Picker is in place for future alternates, though only a single model is currently offered. Downloading the model IS enabling the feature — there is no separate on/off toggle. Two explicit download entry points exist: (1) tapping the "Download · 2.5 GB" CTA on the AI Rewrite settings model strip, and (2) tapping the Rewrite action in the Transcript Detail view when the model is not ready, which opens AI Rewrite settings as a sheet where the same Download CTA lives. Every download CTA and model strip displays the currently-selected model's name and exact size, so the user sees what they are downloading before they tap. The download runs in the foreground; the model strip surfaces a "Keep Jot open while the model downloads" caption under the progress bar to set expectations about backgrounding.
chunks.title: On-Device AI Rewrite Model

chunks.text: Rewrite Trigger from Detail View. From the Transcript Detail view, the accent sparkle-circle Rewrite control in the action bar (an icon-only button, no text label) opens the Prompt Picker so the user can select which rewrite style to apply to the current transcript.
chunks.title: Rewrite Trigger from Detail View

chunks.text: Prompt Picker. A bottom sheet lists all saved rewrite prompts, each with an icon, a name, and a short description. A subline below the prompt list header shows the word count of the source transcript being rewritten and the name of the currently active rewrite model (e.g. "42 words · using Qwen 3.5 4B"). The model name reflects whichever option the user has picked in the Switch Model Picker. The list contains the four built-in default prompts (Cleanup, AI prompt, Action Items, Email) plus any prompts the user has created in Settings → AI. Selecting a prompt applies it to the current transcript. Below the list, a plain centered "+ New prompt" text link opens the New Prompt sheet. A footer note clarifies that rewriting replaces the previous rewrite while leaving the original transcript untouched. See Voice Prompt for the picker's second row, which lets the user *speak* the rewrite instruction instead of picking a saved one. The picker also offers a Translate row — an on-device translate sheet that is *not* a rewrite (it does not save to the transcript).
chunks.title: Prompt Picker

chunks.text: Saved Prompt Management. In Settings → AI, users can view their full list of saved rewrite prompts. The screen leads with an italic serif "AI" title and a small "EXPERIMENTAL" chip to set expectations about feature maturity. Prompts can be reordered by dragging, deleted by swiping, and edited by tapping. Each prompt row shows an icon, the prompt name, and — for the four built-in defaults (Cleanup, AI prompt, Action Items, Email) — a mini before→after sample that previews what the prompt does to a representative transcript. Swiping to delete shows an alert with the prompt's name as the title (e.g. "Delete "My Prompt"?") and the message "This can't be undone." — with a destructive "Delete" button and a "Cancel" button — before the prompt is removed. A "+ New prompt" button at the bottom opens a dedicated New Prompt sheet (see 7.12). Inside the prompt editor for an existing prompt, the system prompt fills the editor as the hero element and a slim "Try this prompt" footer pill at the bottom expands upward into a result panel when tapped — showing the BEFORE transcript, an arrow with run timing, the AFTER rewrite, and Copy + Run again buttons; an "Expand" link opens a full-screen text editor for the instruction. The footer pill defaults to the user's most recent recording, and tapping the recording-name sublabel (marked with a small up/down chevron) opens a recording picker listing recent recordings with a coral checkmark on the currently selected one — picking a different recording updates the BEFORE block and what Run rewrites. A spoken instruction from the Prompt Picker's Voice Prompt row never appears in this list — it applies once and is discarded.
chunks.title: Saved Prompt Management

chunks.text: Model Download Management. Within Settings → AI, a single compact model strip surfaces the active model's name, file size, and a coloured-dot readiness status (ready, downloading with percent, loading, evicted, error, or not downloaded). When the model is not in a ready state, an inline action row appears under the strip in the same card with the contextual control: a "Download · <size>" button for the active model (the size reflects whichever model is currently selected in the Switch Model Picker), a progress bar with Cancel during download, "Loading…" during warm-up, "Reload" after eviction, or "Retry" after an error. All download status lives inside this single strip — there is no separate top-pinned download banner. Long-pressing the model strip opens a context menu with two entries: "Change model" (opens the Switch Model Picker) and a destructive "Delete model" that, after a confirmation dialog naming the model and warning the user they will need to re-download (about 2.5 GB) to use AI rewrite again, purges the on-device model.
